name: Kurichiya
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: Syam, S. K. 2016. Kurichiya Tribe of Kerala - A Phonological Study. Language in India 16(1): 295-306 (January 2016). Data from informants in Mananthavady Taluk, Wayanad.
sources.note: Nothing. Section 2 'Phonology' (pp. 297-305) gives 27 phonemes (5 short + 5 long vowels, 22 consonants) with distribution by word position, consonant clusters, gemination and syllable types (open/closed, mono-/di-/trisyllabic); no suprasegmental, stress, accent, intonation or prosody remark anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent full text: zero hits). Conclusion: 'this language has many similarities with the dialects of Malayalam. More details will be presented in subsequent articles' (p. 305) - no later Kurichiya article by Syam found in Language in India indices 2016-2024.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Kurichiya language' (accessed 2026-09-17), summarising Ethnologue 18 (2015) and Syam 2016.
sources.note: Nothing on stress; reports 'two dialects, Kunnam and Wayanad, are no closer to each other than they are to Malayalam' (from Ethnologue) and the 27-phoneme count from Syam 2016.

sources.citation: Nair, Ravi Sankar S. 2013. Tribal Languages of Kerala. Language in India 13(7), July 2013. Section 'Kurichiya', pp. 33-35.
sources.note: Nothing. 'The Kurichiyar speak a dialect of Malayalam with many phonological peculiarities. Only marginal morphological and syntactic variations from Malayalam are observed' (p. 33); lists segmental correspondences Malayalam > Kurichiya (a>e, i>e, v>b, l>y/v, s>y/c/t, medial consonant elision, tt>rr, r-loss, -nn->-nr-), pronouns, past-tense forms, sentence-final particles. Sole bibliography entry: Vayaleri 1992. No stress/accent mention.

sources.citation: Menon, T. Madhava (ed.). 1996. The Encyclopaedia of Dravidian Tribes, vol. II. Thiruvananthapuram: International School of Dravidian Linguistics. Entries 'KURICHIA' (M. Sasikumar, pp. c.164-169) and 'KURICHIA LANGUAGE' (pp. 169-171).
sources.note: Nothing. Ethnographic entry says 'The Kurichia speak the North Malabar dialect of Malayalam with low content of Sanskrit derived vocabulary and retaining many archaic words.. (Aiyappan 1988:139)'. The 'Kurichia language' entry is the same sketch text as Nair 2013 (segmental correspondences, pronouns, past tense, particles, a few sentences), bibliography = Vayaleri 1992 only; no stress/accent/intonation remark.

sources.citation: Gopalan Nair, C. 1911. Wynad: Its Peoples and Traditions. Madras: Higginbotham. Chapter 'Kurichiyans', pp. 59-64.
sources.note: Nothing. Ethnographic (origin legend, religion, marriage, death, cultivation, caste status); no language section for the Kurichiyans (Glottolog codes it a wordlist or less).

sources.citation: Thurston, Edgar & K. Rangachari. 1909. Castes and Tribes of Southern India, vol. IV. Madras: Government Press. Entry 'Kuricchan', pp. 125-130.
sources.note: Nothing. Ethnographic entry; only linguistic remark is the etymology of the name (kurikke 'to mark', kurissi 'hill'); no language description.

sources.citation: Any follow-up by Syam S. K. (KIRTADS Linguistic Cell, Calicut) on Kurichiya morphology/phonology promised in Syam 2016 ('More details will be presented in subsequent articles'); no such article located in Language in India 2016-2024 indices.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Syam's 2016 paper is the only modern phonological study; a fuller KIRTADS report might include suprasegmentals. Existence unconfirmed.

sources.note: Not opened (not reachable by automated download paywall; Per Wikipedia's summary it lists dialects Kunnam and Wayanad; Ethnologue does not describe stress.

sources.citation: Vayaleri, Kumaran. 1992. Kurichiyarude jivithavum samskaravum [Life and culture of the Kurichiyas]. PhD thesis, Department of Malayalam, University of Calicut (in Malayalam).
sources.note: Unknown. Not on Shodhganga (searches for Kurichiya, Kurichya, Kurichian, Kurichiyarude, Vayaleri returned only anthropology/history theses); no online copy located. It is the sole source cited by both the Nair 2013 and Menon 1996 language sketches, and those sketches contain no stress statement, so its treatment of stress (if any) is unknown.
